title: 01 / A local equipment booking workflow
text: This is CampusGear, a database application developed for the Track One project in Storing and Retrieving Data. The problem is straightforward: shared equipment needs a consistent reservation record, and an item must not be promised to two people for overlapping times. All members and equipment in this demonstration are synthetic. This is a local prototype, not an operational university service. The application runs as one Python process with a SQLite database and a browser interface. We will demonstrate the catalogue, create a reservation, reject a conflict, complete a loan, and inspect the actual database. We will also show measured query performance rather than a simulated dashboard.

title: 02 / Catalogue and relational joins
text: The equipment catalogue is loaded from the backend API. Search and category filters issue real database queries. Each physical item has its own identifier and unique asset tag. Category names are not copied into every reservation: the interface obtains them through relational joins. Members also belong to departments, and a reservation references a member and an item using foreign keys. This keeps descriptive information separate from transaction records. Notice the distinction between equipment condition and reservation status. An item marked available is operational; it does not mean every future time slot is free. Maintenance and retired equipment should not accept new reservations. The member selector is for demonstration, not authentication.

title: 03 / Create a reservation
text: Now we select an available item and a synthetic member, enter a purpose, and choose a future interval. The interface labels the input as UTC. The server requires a canonical timestamp including the final Z, validates that it is a real calendar time, and checks that the start precedes the end. On submission, the browser sends a JSON request. The backend starts a write transaction and inserts a reservation with confirmed status. Database constraints validate the references and values, and a trigger checks for conflicting active reservations. The audit event is recorded with the same transaction. Only after a successful commit does the interface refresh the list. This is the full browser, server, and database path.

title: 04 / Reject overlaps, allow adjacent intervals
text: We now attempt a second reservation for the same equipment and the same time interval. The expected result is a conflict, not a second confirmed booking. This rule is protected in the database rather than only in the web form. Two intervals overlap when the existing start is earlier than the proposed end and the existing end is later than the proposed start. The strict comparisons implement half open intervals. Therefore, a reservation beginning exactly when another ends is allowed. We demonstrate that boundary separately. Cancelled and returned reservations do not block new time slots. This policy is a deliberate prototype rule, and concurrent attempts must still obey it when separate database connections are used.

title: 05 / Checkout, return, and cancellation
text: Next we check out the confirmed reservation. The application creates a loan record and moves the reservation to checked out within one transaction. A reservation can have at most one loan. The application also prevents two open loans for the same physical item, including bookings with otherwise separate planned intervals. For demonstration, early checkout is permitted; a production system would need an approved pickup window. Returning the equipment records an actual return time and moves the reservation to returned. That is different from simply reaching the planned end time. A confirmed reservation may be cancelled, while a checked out item must be returned. Invalid repeated actions are rejected instead of silently changing historical records.

title: 06 / Inspect schema, indexes, and audit events
text: The database inspector reads table and index definitions from SQLite itself. It is not a hard coded picture of the schema. The main relations cover departments, members, categories, equipment, reservations, loans, and audit events. Primary keys identify rows; foreign keys link them. Unique constraints protect asset tags and the one loan per reservation rule. Check constraints restrict domains. Triggers handle the cross row overlap rule that an ordinary row check cannot express. The audit view exposes the effects of our actual actions. This event log helps explain what happened, but it is not a tamper proof security ledger. The application deliberately separates planned reservation times from actual loan timestamps and calculates overdue loans from those facts.

title: 07 / Correctness and measured query performance
text: Evaluation has two parts. Correctness tests exercise successful operations and rejected boundary cases, including overlap protection, adjacent intervals, state transitions, malformed timestamps, foreign keys, and concurrent requests. The included test output records the real run. The benchmark generates deterministic synthetic reservations at three scales: one thousand, ten thousand, and one hundred thousand rows. It measures the same overlap query without and with the target index, confirms equal results, and records repeated timings and query plans. The report contains the actual measurements. These are warm cache query microbenchmarks on one machine, not network load tests or proof of campus wide scalability. Index maintenance and write costs remain relevant, and the speedup applies only to the measured workload.

title: 08 / Limitations and reproducibility
text: The main result is a reproducible local application whose database protects a meaningful workflow. It is intentionally not production ready. There is no real login, student versus administrator authorization, single sign on, email notification, payment handling, or deployment hardening. Python's built in HTTP server is used to keep the course demonstration dependency free, and the service binds only to the local machine. The source package includes the schema, backend, frontend, test suite, data generation, benchmark code, and running instructions. The report documents the architecture, design decisions, measured results, and limitations. Before submission, the group must confirm its real members and contributions and provide accessible repository and video links. AI assistance is disclosed rather than attributed to fictional student work.
